column2: Likewise Kritavarman, fighting Shaineya, scorcher of foes, shone, O king, like Shakra in battle with an army.
Duryodhana, cutting Dhrishtadyumna's bow in the battle, then pierced him, bowless, with sharp arrows.
Dhrishtadyumna too in the battle, taking a supreme weapon, fought the king in the sight of all bowmen.
A great battle took place between them, O best of the Bharatas, like two rutting great elephants locked together.
Gautama (Kripa), enraged in the battle, the hero, pierced the mighty sons of Draupadi with many straight-jointed arrows.
His battle with them was like that of the embodied with the senses, dreadful, irresistible and utterly without restraint.
They tormented him as the senses a fool; and he, enraged, fought them back in the battle.
Thus wondrous was his battle with them, O Bharata, as the embodied rising again and again against their senses, lord.
Men fought with men, elephants with elephants, horses with horses, chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, and the confusion became yet more dreadful, O lord of men.
This is wondrous, this dreadful, this fierce, O lord—many dreadful battles took place, O great king.
Meeting each other in the battle, the tamers of foes pierced and slew one another in the great fight.
The fierce dust raised by them was seen, driven by the wind, O king, and by horsemen running.
Raised by wheel-rims and the breath of elephants, the dust, tawny like the evening cloud, rose to the sun's path.
With the sun joined with that dust and dimmed, the earth and those brave great chariot-warriors were covered.
In a moment all became free of dust on every side; on the ground drenched with the blood of heroes, O best of the Bharatas, that dreadful-looking fierce dust subsided.
Then I saw, O great king, duels, O Bharata, each best to best, eldest to eldest, in the very terrible noon; the bright lustre of armour was seen there, O king of kings.
A very tumultuous sound of falling arrows arose in the battle, like that of a great bamboo grove burning on every side.
Holding off those great chariot-warriors with great effort, your son fought the Pandava army.
The warriors who suddenly turned back, wishing their dear one, your son, well—when they had turned back, a very dreadful battle took place.
It was like the war of gods and asuras, of yours and the enemy; none of the enemy or of your army was turned away.
They fought by inference and by signs with one another; a great destruction took place among those fighting each other.
Then King Yudhishthira, filled with great anger, desiring victory over Dhritarashtra's sons and their kings in the battle,
piercing Sharadvata (Kripa) with three gold-feathered stone-whetted arrows, killed Kritavarman's four fine horses with four.
Ashvatthaman carried the renowned Hardikya away; then Sharadvata pierced Yudhishthira in return with eight.
Then King Duryodhana sent seven hundred chariots in the battle to where the king, the son of Dharma Yudhishthira, was.
Those chariots, manned by chariot-warriors, swift as mind and wind, rushed in the battle at the son of Kunti's chariot.
They surrounded Yudhishthira on every side, O great king, and made him invisible with arrows, like clouds the sun.
The chariot-warriors led by Shikhandin, much enraged, could not bear it; they came with chariots of the fastest speed, covered with nets of little bells, protecting Kunti's son Yudhishthira.
Then a dreadful battle began, with blood for water, of the Pandavas and the Kurus, increasing the realm of Yama.
Having slain seven hundred chariots of the aggressor Kurus, the Pandavas with the Panchalas again held them back.
There was a great battle of your son with the Pandavas; we have never seen nor heard the like.
While the battle went on thus without restraint on every side, with warriors being slain, yours and others,
with the warriors roaring and excellent conches filled, shouted lion-roars and the roar of bowmen,
with the battle at its height, vital parts being cut and warriors running eager for victory, O revered one,
with destruction on every side, a cause of sorrow on earth, and the parting-lines of many noble women being cleared,
while the unrestrained, most dreadful battle went on, terrible portents appeared for destruction; the earth with its mountains and forests shook with sound.
Meteors with staffs and firebrands, O king, falling scattered on every side from the sky to earth, striking the sun's disc.
Winds blew in all directions, raining gravel low; elephants shed tears and a trembling touched them hard.
Disregarding these dreadful, most terrible portents, the kshatriyas, conferring together, stood again undismayed for battle, desiring heaven on the lovely holy Kurukshetra.
Then Shakuni, son of the king of Gandhara, said, "Fight in front, while I kill the Pandavas from behind."
Then, as we advanced, the mighty Madra warriors, delighted, raised a clamour, and others too.
Meeting us again, unassailable, having attained their aims, shaking their bows, they covered us with showers of arrows.
Then the force of the king of the Madras was slain there by the enemy, and seeing it Duryodhana's army again turned away.
The king of Gandhara, strong, said again, "Turn back, you who do not know dharma! Fight; what is flight to you?"
The king of Gandhara had a force of ten thousand horse, lancers with spotless lances, O best of the Bharatas.
With that force he showed valour while the slaughter went on and struck the Pandava army from behind with sharp arrows.
Tossed on all sides like a cloud by wind, the great Pandava force broke, O great king.
Then Yudhishthira, seeing his force broken nearby, unflurried, urged the mighty Sahadeva:

There Subala's son, armoured, harassing our rear, slays the army; see, Pandava, the ill-minded one.
mahabharata:9:22.34	Go, and the sons of Draupadi, and slay Shakuni son of Subala; I shall guard the chariot-force with the Panchalas, sinless one.
mahabharata:9:22.35	Let all the elephants go and the horses with you, and three thousand foot-soldiers; slay Shakuni son of Subala.
Then seven hundred elephants manned by bowmen, five thousand horses and the valiant Sahadeva,
three thousand foot-soldiers and all the sons of Draupadi rushed at Shakuni, arrogant in battle.
Then Subala's son, O king, passing the Pandavas, the glorious, eager for victory, struck the army from behind.
The enraged horsemen of the strong Pandavas entered the force of Subala's son, passing those chariots.
Those brave horsemen there stood in the midst of the great force of Subala's son and covered them with showers of arrows.
A great battle took place, with maces and lances raised, attended by the unwavering, O king, through your ill counsel.
The cries of victory ceased and the chariot-warriors became spectators, for no distinction was seen between their own and the enemy.
The Kurus and Pandavas saw the falling of darts hurled from the arms of the brave like falling of luminaries.
With rishtis and bright swords falling here and there, O lord of men, the sky covered by them shone much.
The appearance of falling lances all around, O king, was like locusts in the sky, O best of the Bharatas.
Horses with all limbs smeared with blood, their riders thrown, fell by hundreds and thousands.
Crushed together, meeting one another, unwounded they were seen vomiting blood from their mouths.
Then a dreadful darkness came, the army covered with dust; I saw those tamers of foes retreating from that place, horses and men, with the dust covering.
Others fell on the ground vomiting much blood; hair tangled in hair, men could not move.
Dragging each other from horses' backs, strong ones like wrestlers meeting struck each other; many were dragged by horses there, lifeless.
Many others, wishing victory, fell on the ground; men thinking themselves heroes were seen here and there.
The earth was seen strewn by hundreds and thousands with blood-smeared bodies, severed arms and dragged hair.
One could not go far there on any horse, the ground being covered with slain horses and horsemen.
With blood-smeared armour, taking weapons, raising them, with dreadful weapons of many kinds, wishing each other's death, closely engaged, the soldiers mostly slain in the battle,
after fighting a moment, Subala's son, O lord of men, withdrew with six thousand surviving horses.
Likewise the Pandava force, drenched in blood, withdrew with six thousand surviving horses, their mounts weary.
The Pandava horsemen, smeared with blood, closely engaged in battle and mostly given up life, said:

It is not possible here to fight with chariots, how then with great elephants? Let chariots go only against chariots and elephants against elephants.
mahabharata:9:22.59	Shakuni has returned and stands by his own force; Subala's king will not come to battle again.
Then the sons of Draupadi and those rutting great elephants went to where the Panchala Dhrishtadyumna, the great chariot-warrior, was.
Sahadeva too, O Kaurava, as the cloud of dust rose, went alone to where King Yudhishthira was.
When they had gone, Shakuni, Subala's son, enraged, again struck Dhrishtadyumna's force from the side.
That again became a tumultuous battle, with yours and the enemy abandoning life, each wishing the other's death.
They looked at one another in that meeting of heroes; warriors fell, O king, by hundreds and thousands.
As heads were cut by swords, at the destruction of the world a great sound arose like palms falling.
Of bodies released, split and falling to the ground, with weapons, of arms and thighs, O lord of men, there was a clattering sound, very great and hair-raising.
Striking brothers, sons and friends with sharp weapons, warriors fell like birds for meat.
Enraged at one another, meeting each other, "I first! I first!" they struck by thousands.
With heaps of horsemen thrown from their seats and lifeless, horses fell by hundreds and thousands.
Of the crushed, quivering, swift-running horses and the groaning armoured men, O lord of men,
a tumultuous noise of darts, rishtis and lances arose, splitting vitals, O king, through your ill counsel.
Overcome with fatigue, enraged, their mounts weary, thirsty and wounded by sharp weapons, yours advanced.
Many there, intoxicated by the smell of blood and senseless, killed enemy and their own, whoever was nearest.
Many kshatriyas eager for victory, their breath gone, fell on the ground, O king, covered with showers of arrows.
On that tumultuous, joyful day for wolves, vultures and jackals, a dreadful destruction of the force took place in your son's sight.
The earth was covered with bodies of men and horses, O lord of men, variegated with floods of blood, increasing the fear of the timid.
Being hewed again and again by swords and pattishas of the brave, yours and the Pandavas did not retreat, O Bharata.
Striking according to their strength, so long as life was held, warriors fell, vomiting blood from their wounds.
A headless trunk was seen holding a head by its hair, raising a sharp sword smeared with blood.
Then when many trunks had risen, O lord of men, and from the smell of blood, the warriors fell into stupor.
Then, when the sound had grown faint, Subala's son advanced against the great Pandava force with the few remaining horses.
Then the Pandavas, quickly, eager for victory, foot-soldiers, elephants and horsemen with weapons raised, rushed at him.
Surrounding him on all sides as in a pen, they struck him with weapons of many kinds, wishing to cross the farther shore of the battle.
Seeing them rushing on every side, yours with horses, foot-soldiers, elephants and chariots rushed at the Pandavas.
Some foot-soldiers, brave in battle, struck each other with feet and fists, their weapons spent, and then fell.
Chariot-warriors fell from chariots, elephant-riders from elephants, like siddhas fallen from celestial cars when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, exerting themselves, warriors slew in the great battle fathers, brothers, friends and sons.
Thus the unrestrained battle went on, O best of the Bharatas, in the most dreadful mire of lances, swords and arrows.
Going swiftly to the army, he said, urging in the battle, "Fight!", delighted again and again, tamer of foes; and he asked the kshatriyas there, "Where is the king, the great chariot-warrior?"
Hearing Shakuni's words, they said, O best of the Bharatas, "There stands the Kaurava, the great chariot-warrior, in the midst of the battle,
where that great parasol shines like the full moon, where those chariots stand armoured, protecting the ground,
and where this tumultuous sound like the roar of a cloud is—go there swiftly, king, and you will see the Kaurava."
Thus addressed by those brave ones, Shakuni son of Subala went to where your son was, O lord of men, surrounded on all sides by heroes who never retreat in battles.
Then, seeing Duryodhana stationed in the chariot-force, Shakuni gladdened all your men and chariot-warriors.
Joyful, he said to Duryodhana, thinking himself to have accomplished his task:
Slay the chariot-force, O king; I have conquered all the horses; Yudhishthira cannot be conquered in battle without giving up life.
Hearing his words, your men, eager for victory, glad, rushed with speed at the Pandava army.
All with quivers open and bows taken, shaking their bows, raised lion-roars.
Then, O lord of men, the sound of bowstrings arose again, and the dreadful sound of arrows well loosed.
Seeing them near, swiftly with raised bows, Dhananjaya son of Kunti said to Devaki's son:

Urge the horses without alarm; enter this ocean of force. Today I shall end the foes with sharp arrows.
mahabharata:9:23.16	Today, Janardana, is the eighteenth day of this great battle, which has gone on, with their meeting one another.
mahabharata:9:23.17	An army that was endless, of these great souls, has gone to destruction in the battle; see, fate is what it is.
mahabharata:9:23.18	The force of Dhritarashtra's son like an ocean, Madhava, reaching us has become like a cow's hoofprint, Achyuta.
mahabharata:9:23.19	When Bhishma was slain he might have made peace, and there would be welfare here, Madhava; but the foolish Dhritarashtra's son, very childish, did not do so.
mahabharata:9:23.20	The wholesome, beneficial word spoken by Bhishma, Madhava, that too he did not follow, Suyodhana, void of sense.
mahabharata:9:23.21	When Bhishma fell, fallen on the surface of the earth, I do not know what cause the battle continued.
mahabharata:9:23.22	I deem Dhritarashtra's sons utterly foolish and childish, who made war again when the son of Shantanu had fallen.
mahabharata:9:23.23	Then when Drona, best of Brahma's knowers, was slain, and Radheya and Vikarna, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.24	When this army was reduced to a remnant, and the charioteer's son felled with his son, the tiger among men, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.25	When the brave Shrutayus was slain, and Jalasandha the Paurava, and King Shrutayudha, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.26	When Bhurishravas, Shalya, the Shalva, Janardana, and the Avanti heroes were slain, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.27	When Jayadratha was slain, and the rakshasa Alayudha, Bahlika and Somadatta, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.28	When the brave Bhagadatta was slain, and the Kamboja Sudakshina, and Duhshasana, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.29	Seeing the brave slain, separately, with the provincial kings, and the strong in battle, Krishna, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.30	Seeing the lords of akshauhinis felled by Bhimasena, whether through delusion or greed, the slaughter did not cease.
mahabharata:9:23.31	Who else born in a royal family, especially a Kaurava, would make a great useless enmity other than Suyodhana?
mahabharata:9:23.32	Knowing the others superior in qualities, strength and valour, what wise man would fight, knowing what is beneficial and harmful?
mahabharata:9:23.33	He whose mind did not turn to the wholesome word you spoke for peace with the Pandavas, how would he listen to another?
mahabharata:9:23.34	By whom Bhishma son of Shantanu, Drona and Vidura were refused regarding peace, what remedy is there for him today?
mahabharata:9:23.35	By folly he refused his aged father, Janardana, and his mother speaking wholesome words, wishing him well; he refused them without respect; to whom would he listen?
mahabharata:9:23.36	This battle, Janardana, clearly is the destroyer of the family, and his conduct and policy are seen, O lord of men; I think, Achyuta, he will not give us the kingdom.
mahabharata:9:23.37	I was told many times, dear one, by the great-souled Vidura: 'Dhritarashtra's son will not give a share while he lives, in any way.
mahabharata:9:23.38	As long as his breath is drawn, giver of honour, he will practise sin against you sinless ones.'
mahabharata:9:23.39	'He is not to be conquered otherwise except by the aged one, Madhava'—so Vidura, who sees the truth, always told me.
mahabharata:9:23.40	All that I know today, the resolve of the evil-souled one, what was said by the great-souled Vidura.
mahabharata:9:23.41	He who, hearing wholesome words truly from Jamadagni's son, slighted them, ill-minded, is surely at death's mouth.
mahabharata:9:23.42	It was said by many siddhas when Suyodhana was just born: 'Reaching this evil-souled one, the kshatra will go to destruction.'
mahabharata:9:23.43	That saying of theirs, Janardana, is explained: the kings have gone to utter destruction for Duryodhana's sake.
mahabharata:9:23.44	Today I shall slay all the warriors in the battle, Madhava; with the kshatriyas quickly slain and the camp emptied,
mahabharata:9:23.45	he will choose battle with us for his own death; by inference, Madhava, the enmity would end there.
mahabharata:9:23.46	Thus I see, Varshneya, reflecting with my own intelligence and by Vidura's word and the evil-souled one's conduct.
mahabharata:9:23.47	Drive on, hero, to the Bharata force, until I slay with sharp arrows the evil-souled Duryodhana and his army in the battle.
mahabharata:9:23.48	Today I shall make safety for the king of dharma, Madhava, having slain this weak force of Dhritarashtra's son in his sight.
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed by Savyasachin, the Dasharha, rein in hand, fearless, entered the flood of the foes' force in the battle.
The dreadful excellent bow, covered with dart-thorns, with paths of maces and clubs, with chariots and elephants as great trees,
strewn with horses and foot-soldiers as creepers—plunging into it, the greatly renowned Govinda ranged there in his chariot with many banners.
Those white horses, O king, carrying Arjuna in the battle, urged by the Dasharha, were seen in all quarters.
Then Savyasachin, scorcher of foes, went in his chariot in the battle, scattering hundreds of sharp arrows, like a cloud streams of water.
A great sound arose of straight-jointed arrows, as the armies were covered by Savyasachin in the battle.
Floods of arrows fell on the ground, not clinging to armour, arrows loosed from Gandiva, touching like Indra's thunderbolt.
Striking men, elephants and horses, O lord of men, the arrows fell in the battle, roaring like moths.
Everything was covered by arrows loosed from Gandiva; in the battle neither quarters nor intermediate quarters could be distinguished.
The whole world was filled with arrows marked with Partha's name, gold-feathered, washed in oil, polished by smiths.
Burned by Partha, the Kauravas, like elephants by fire, pressed together, being slain by sharp arrows.
Partha, bearing bow and arrows, as if blazing, O Bharata, burned the warriors in the battle as fire burns dry grass.
As a fire in a forest's end, released by foresters, burns dry grass with Krishna's path and noise, a great tree with dry creepers spread, a blazing fire grown mighty, scorching,
so he, scorching with masses of iron arrows, with flames of arrows of keen varying splendour, burned all your son's army, impatient, swift and mighty.
His arrows, life-taking and well loosed, did not catch on armour, gold-feathered; he did not loose a second arrow at any man, horse or great elephant.
Entering the great chariot-force with arrows of many forms, that one alone slew your son's army, like the thunderbolt-wielder daityas.
He was seen loosing arrows of great vigour, unbearable, touching like Indra's thunderbolt, streaming like a cloud.
That army, O best of the Bharatas, being slain by Kiritin, fled from the battle in the sight of your son.
Some chariots had their yokes-bearers slain, others their charioteers, some had broken axles, yokes, wheels and poles, O lord of men.
Others had arrows spent, others were afflicted by arrows, some unwounded fled together, afflicted by fear.
He could not sleep, burning with great rage, and looked at that forest of dreadful aspect, mighty-armed.
By you and by your son, fanned by the wind of words, and sprinkled with the ghee of greed, this fire of Partha has been kindled.
Only five sons will you have, mother, surely; either with Karna if Partha is slain, or with Arjuna if I am slain.
As in the making of a clay pot the rod, wheel and the rest are reckoned as causes, so you too, serpent, are a cause.
By what deed I might be freed from this cruel act, tamer of foes, ordain that deed here, by which my mind may be purified.
As long as the chief of the Kurus' son lived, whatever happiness there was, let him obtain it and enjoyments—so they resolved.
White-and-red-footed birds, urged by time, doves ranged in the houses of the Vrishnis and Andhakas.
Then the god of seven flames (Agni) said to the Pandavas, "O Pandava heroes, do not disturb Fire."
Wherever he stays, I wish to see the sun's son, whom I did not know and who was slain by Savyasachin.
